recipes.name: Salade Lyonnaise
recipes.flavorProfile: Bitter dandelion or frisée leaves dressed in vinaigrette and wilted by hot smoky lardons, with a soft poached egg breaking over everything.
recipes.healthBenefit: Dandelion greens are rich in vitamin K, vitamin A and calcium and the egg brings protein; the bacon makes it hearty, so it is a meal in itself.

ingredients.cutPrep: washed and dried, or curly endive (frisée)

instructions: Cook the lardons in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until golden. Keep them warm.
Bring a wide pan of water to a bare simmer. Break in the eggs one at a time and poach 3 to 4 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks soft. Lift out and drain on paper towels.
Toss the greens with the vinaigrette and divide between plates.
Scatter over the hot lardons, set a poached egg on each plate, grind over pepper and serve at once.

nutritionHighlights.note: Dandelion greens carry a great deal.
From the dandelion greens and egg yolk.

recipes.curationNote: 750g, Salade lyonnaise for every amount and step; serves 4: 400 g dandelion, 4 eggs, 200 g smoked bacon, a vinaigrette of 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 level tsp strong mustard, 1 tbsp wine vinegar, salt and pepper; no croutons and no parsley.

recipes.name: Céleri Rémoulade
recipes.flavorProfile: Fine crunchy threads of raw celeriac, nutty and fresh, coated in a sharp mustardy mayonnaise and brightened with lemon.
recipes.healthBenefit: Celeriac brings fibre, potassium and vitamin K; the mayonnaise makes it rich, so a modest spoonful as a starter suits it best.

ingredients.cutPrep: peeled and finely grated or cut in thin julienne

instructions: Peel the celeriac, grate it finely or cut it into thin matchsticks, and toss it at once with half the lemon juice so it stays white.
Stir the mustard into the mayonnaise with the rest of the lemon juice.
Fold the sauce into the celeriac a little at a time, just enough to coat it without leaving sauce in the bottom of the bowl.
Season with salt and pepper, scatter with parsley and chill 30 minutes to 1 hour before serving as a starter.
recipes.curationNote: The 750g recipe gives 600 g celeriac, mayonnaise, strong mustard, lemon and parsley for 4. Etchebest confirms finely grated celeriac, citrus to keep it white, mustard folded into a homemade mayonnaise and no sauce pooling at the bottom; his green apple was left out as a personal touch. The mayonnaise points at the base.

recipes.name: Carottes Râpées
recipes.flavorProfile: Sweet, crunchy grated carrot in a bright lemon and mustard dressing with parsley, a pinch of cumin and plump raisins.
recipes.healthBenefit: Raw carrots are full of beta-carotene, which the olive oil in the dressing helps the body take up, and they bring fibre and potassium.
instructions: Peel and finely grate the carrots into a salad bowl. Add the parsley and raisins.
Whisk the mustard, lemon juice, cumin, salt and pepper together, then whisk in the olive oil until the dressing thickens.
Pour the dressing over the carrots and toss well.
Leave 10 to 15 minutes before serving so the carrots soak up the dressing.

citations.source: La Cuisine de Géraldine, Grated carrots with lemon and cumin
750g, Carottes râpées au cumin et à l'orange

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine gives 500 g carrots, parsley, raisins and a lemon, Dijon and olive oil dressing with a pinch of cumin, rested 10 minutes. The 750g version confirms an oil and acid dressing with cumin (it uses orange and vinegar). Géraldine's optional honey was left out.

recipes.name: Salade de Chèvre Chaud
recipes.flavorProfile: Crisp dressed leaves under warm toasts of country bread topped with soft, tangy goat cheese just starting to melt, with a grind of black pepper.
recipes.healthBenefit: Goat cheese brings protein and calcium and the leaves bring folate and vitamin K; cheese on bread makes it filling, so it works as a light meal.
instructions: Heat the oven to 320°F (160°C). Set two discs of goat cheese on each slice of bread and lay them on a baking sheet lined with parchment.
Bake about 10 minutes, until the cheese starts to melt.
Meanwhile toss the leaves with the vinaigrette and divide between plates.
Grind pepper over each hot toast, set it on the salad and serve at once.
recipes.curationNote: 750g, Salade de chèvre chaud for every amount and step; serves 2: 140 g crottin, 2 slices country bread, 4 lettuce leaves, a vinaigrette of 1 tsp mustard, 4 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp white wine vinegar, salt and pepper; 160°C for about 10 minutes; no honey and no herbs. Doubled for our 4.

recipes.name: Salade de Lentilles
recipes.flavorProfile: Firm, earthy green lentils dressed while warm in a sharp mustard and shallot vinaigrette, with diced carrot and plenty of chives and parsley.
recipes.healthBenefit: Lentils bring plant protein, fibre, iron and folate, and dressing them with vinegar and herbs keeps the dish light and fresh.
instructions: Put the lentils and carrot in a saucepan, cover with cold water and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer about 20 minutes, until tender but whole. Salt in the last 5 minutes.
Drain well.
Stir the shallot into the vinaigrette and pour it over the lentils while they are still warm, so they take it in.
Leave to cool to room temperature, then fold in the chives and parsley and season with pepper. Serve tepid or cool.

nutritionHighlights.note: Lentils are one of the best plant sources.

citations.source: 750g, Salade de lentilles aux herbes fraîches

recipes.curationNote: 750g, Salade de lentilles aux herbes fraîches for every amount and step; serves 4: 250 g lentils, 1 carrot, 60 cl water, 1 shallot, 1 bunch chives, 5 sprigs flat parsley; vinaigrette of 6 tbsp olive oil, 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tsp mustard, salt and pepper to taste; no thyme or bay.

recipes.name: Baguette
recipes.flavorProfile: A crackling golden crust with sharp scored ears and a creamy, open, faintly sweet crumb that tastes of wheat.
recipes.healthBenefit: Made from nothing but flour, water, yeast and salt, it carries no fat or sugar; it is mostly starch, so it sits best beside protein and vegetables.

ingredients.baseName: Grains, wheat flour, white, bread flour

instructions: Mix the flour and 330 ml of the water until no dry flour is left, then rest 20 to 30 minutes so the flour drinks the water.
Dissolve the yeast in the last 20 ml of water and work it in with the salt. Knead 5 to 8 minutes until smooth.
Rise 1 hour in a covered bowl, giving the dough a stretch and fold every 20 minutes (3 in all). Then leave it another 1 to 1.5 hours until airy.
Divide in two, pre-shape each into a loose log and rest 20 minutes. Shape into long baguettes about 50 to 60 cm and lay them seam up in a floured cloth folded between them. Proof 20 to 40 minutes.

Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) with a baking stone or tray inside and a tray for water below. Roll the loaves onto a floured peel, seam down, and score 5 or 6 long slashes at a shallow 45 degree angle.

Slide them in, pour a glass of hot water into the lower tray for steam, and bake 20 to 25 minutes, lowering to 425°F (220°C) after the first 5 minutes, until deep gold and hollow when tapped. Cool on a rack.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the wheat flour, the main fuel in the loaf.
The tradition recipe allows no fat at all.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia gives the 1993 décret pain tradition rule (only flour, water, yeast or levain, and salt), a loaf of about 250 g, 45 degree scoring and steam. 750g gave the proportions (500 g T55, 350 g water, 7 g each of salt and fresh yeast for 2 baguettes), the three folds 20 minutes apart and the 230 then 220°C bake. Each baguette is cut in 4, so one serving is a quarter loaf.

recipes.name: Pain de Campagne
recipes.flavorProfile: A thick floury crust over a greyish, chewy crumb with the slightly sour, earthy taste the rye brings.
recipes.healthBenefit: The rye flour adds fibre and minerals that white flour lacks, and the bread has no fat; one slice is mostly starch, so it pairs well with soups and salads.

ingredients.baseName: Grains, wheat flour, white, bread flour

instructions: Dissolve the yeast and sugar in a little of the warm water. Mix the two flours with the salt, add the yeast and the rest of the water and knead 10 to 12 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky.
Cover and rise 1 to 1.5 hours in a warm place, until doubled.
Knock back, shape into a tight round or oval loaf and set it on a floured tray or in a floured basket. Proof 30 to 45 minutes.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a tray of water on the lowest shelf. Dust the loaf with flour and score a cross or a few long slashes.
Bake 30 minutes with the water, then take the water out and bake another 10 to 15 minutes, until the crust is dark and the base sounds hollow. Cool fully before slicing into about 16 slices.
recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes pain de campagne as a wheat loaf with a share of rye, often made with levain and finished with a dusting of flour. 750g gave the yeasted home version used here: 375 g T65, 125 g rye T130, 300 ml water, 20 g fresh yeast, 10 g salt, 5 g sugar, with a water tray for the first 30 minutes at 220°C. Cut into 16 slices so the chèvre chaud salad can point at 4 of them.

recipes.name: Brioche
recipes.flavorProfile: A shiny mahogany crust and a feathery, buttery, gently sweet crumb that pulls apart in strands.
recipes.healthBenefit: Eggs and milk give it some protein, but with this much butter and sugar it is a rich bread, best kept for a weekend breakfast or a treat.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.cutPrep: beaten with a spoon of milk, to glaze

instructions: Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk. Put the flour, sugar and salt in a mixer bowl (salt away from the yeast), add the milk and eggs and knead on low 5 minutes, then on medium 5 minutes.
Add the soft butter a piece at a time and knead another 10 to 12 minutes, until the dough comes away from the bowl and stretches thin without tearing.
Cover and rise 1.5 to 2 hours at room temperature, knock back, then chill 2 hours or overnight so the butter firms and the dough is easy to shape.
Divide into 8 balls of about 75 g and set them in two rows in a buttered loaf tin. Proof 45 to 60 minutes, until they reach the rim.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C), or 330°F (165°C) with fan. Brush the top with the yolk and milk and bake 22 to 25 minutes, until deep gold. Unmould and cool on a rack.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the butter, which makes this a rich bread.

citations.source: La Cuisine de Géraldine, French brioche

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia gives the definition (a leavened dough rich in egg and butter, at least 400 g butter per kg of flour for the name pur beurre) and the Nanterre shape of balls side by side in a mould with an egg glaze. Géraldine gave the quantities for 8: 350 g flour, 120 g butter, 120 g egg, 80 ml milk, 50 g sugar, 13 g fresh yeast, 6 g salt, the long kneading, the cold rest and 22 to 25 minutes at 165°C fan.

recipes.name: Croissants
recipes.flavorProfile: Shattering, deep golden layers outside and a honeycomb of soft buttery dough inside, lightly sweet and salty.
recipes.healthBenefit: Almost a third of the weight is butter, so a croissant is a rich treat for an occasional breakfast rather than an everyday bread.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.cutPrep: beaten with 30 ml milk, to glaze

instructions: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, salt, cold water, cold milk and 50 g soft butter into a smooth dough, 5 to 8 minutes. Flatten it into a rectangle, wrap and chill 1 to 2 hours.
Beat the 250 g cold butter between two sheets of baking paper into a flat square about 1 cm thick, still cold but pliable. Chill it beside the dough.
Roll the dough to a rectangle twice the size of the butter, set the butter in the middle and fold the dough over it to seal it in.

Roll out to a long strip and give a double fold (both ends to the middle, then closed like a book). Wrap and chill 30 to 60 minutes. Roll out again and give a single fold in three. Wrap and chill overnight.

Roll the dough to about 4 mm thick and cut long triangles with a base of 8 to 10 cm. Make a small cut in the middle of each base, then roll each triangle from the base to the tip and set it on a tray with the tip underneath.
Proof 1 to 1.5 hours somewhere warm, 80 to 85°F (27 to 30°C) and no warmer or the butter melts out, until wobbly and nearly doubled.
Heat the oven to 375 to 390°F (190 to 200°C), or 355°F (180°C) with fan. Brush gently with the yolk and milk and bake 15 to 20 minutes, until deep golden. Cool on a rack 10 minutes before eating.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the butter that makes the layers.
From the wheat flour and sugar.

citations.source: La Cuisine de Géraldine, Homemade croissants

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes the croissant as a laminated yeasted dough, traces it to the Viennese bakery of August Zang in Paris in 1837 to 1839 and to the first laminated recipes around 1905, and gives a warm proof and a bake near 180°C. Géraldine gave the recipe: 500 g flour, 7 g dry yeast, 60 g sugar, 10 g salt, 140 g each of cold water and milk, 50 g butter in the dough, a 250 g butter block, one double fold and one single fold, an overnight rest, a 27 to 30°C proof and 15 to 20 minutes. Her recipe says it serves 8; at the usual 4 mm and 8 to 10 cm triangles this much dough makes about 12, which is the count used.

recipes.name: Pain au Chocolat
recipes.flavorProfile: Flaky buttery layers wrapped around two bars of dark chocolate that soften as it bakes.
recipes.healthBenefit: Dark chocolate brings a little iron and magnesium, but with the butter and sugar this is a rich pastry for now and then.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

ingredients.cutPrep: soft enough to bend, for the folding

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Mix the flour, sugar, salt, yeast and warm milk into a smooth ball, 5 to 8 minutes. Wrap and chill at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Roll the dough into a square. Set the butter, flattened to the same softness as the dough, in the middle and fold the four sides over it to enclose it.
Roll out into a long strip, fold in three and chill 15 to 20 minutes. Repeat twice more, chilling 20 minutes after the second fold and at least 1 hour after the third.

Roll the dough 3 to 4 mm thick and cut strips a little longer than the chocolate bâtons and about 8 cm wide. Lay a bâton at one end, fold the dough over it, set a second bâton against the fold and roll up, finishing with the seam underneath.
Set on lined trays, cover loosely and proof 1.5 to 2 hours somewhere warm, until doubled. Heat the oven to 355°F (180°C).
Brush with beaten egg and bake 15 to 20 minutes, until deep gold. Cool a little before eating.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the butter that makes the layers.
A small amount from the dark chocolate.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia: the pain au chocolat (chocolatine across the Southwest) is croissant dough, rectangular, rolled around one or more bars of chocolate; the first versions by Zang and Schwarzer used brioche dough. 750g gave the recipe used: 500 g flour, 220 g butter, 40 g sugar, 28 cl milk, 10 g fresh yeast, 2 tsp salt, three folds with the rests named, 2 bâtons per pastry and 15 to 20 minutes at 180°C. 750g left the chocolate quantity open; 24 bâtons of about 5 g is the standard for this much dough.

recipes.name: Fougasse
recipes.flavorProfile: A flat leaf-shaped bread with crisp edges round its open slashes, soft inside, fragrant with olive oil, black olives and thyme.
recipes.healthBenefit: Olive oil brings mostly monounsaturated fat and the olives add a little vitamin E; it is still mostly white flour, so a piece goes best with a salad or soup.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

ingredients.cutPrep: black olives, pitted and roughly chopped

instructions: Dissolve the yeast in the warm water. Mix with the flour, salt and 4 tbsp olive oil and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and supple.
Work in the olives and thyme, cover and rise about 1 hour, until doubled.

Divide into 4 and flatten each into an oval about 1.5 cm thick on a lined tray. With a sharp knife or a dough scraper cut a long slit down the middle and 3 or 4 slanting slits each side, cutting right through, and pull them open with your fingers so they will not close in the oven.
Cover and rest 45 minutes to 1 hour. Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a dish of water on the bottom shelf.
Brush with the remaining olive oil and bake 15 to 20 minutes, until golden. Each fougasse is torn into 2 pieces at the table.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the olive oil and olives.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia: a Provençal flat bread of wheat flour, baker's yeast and olive oil, cut open like branches, garnished with olives, onions, anchovies or herbes de Provence. 750g's olive fougasse (750 g flour, 15 g yeast, 9 tbsp olive oil, 250 g olives, thyme, 1 hour rise, 6 slashed ovals, 1 hour rest, 200°C with water for about 15 minutes) is scaled here to 500 g flour, making 4 fougasses of 2 pieces each.

recipes.name: Pain d'Épices
recipes.flavorProfile: A dense, moist, honey-dark loaf warm with cinnamon, ginger and quatre-épices, better after a day or two wrapped up.
recipes.healthBenefit: Rye flour brings fibre and the spices bring their aroma with no fat to speak of, but the honey makes it a sweet, so a thin slice is the way to eat it.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.cutPrep: plus a little for the tin

instructions: Heat the oven to 320°F (160°C) and butter and line a loaf tin about 25 cm long.

Warm the cinnamon, ginger and quatre-épices in a small pan for a few seconds until they smell toasted. Add the milk, honey, sugar and butter and heat gently, stirring, just until everything melts. Do not boil.
Mix the two flours with the baking powder in a bowl, pour in the warm honey mixture and stir to a smooth, thick batter.
Pour into the tin and bake 40 to 50 minutes, until dark brown and a skewer comes out clean. Cover loosely with foil if the top darkens too fast.
Cool in the tin 10 minutes, then on a rack. Wrap it and keep it 1 to 2 days before slicing; it grows moister and the spices deepen.

nutritionHighlights.note: From the honey and cassonade, which make it a sweet.

citations.source: 750g, Le pain d'épices maison de Philippe Etchebest

recipes.curationNote: 750g, Le pain d'épices maison de Philippe Etchebest for every amount and step; 250 g honey, 100 g cassonade, 125 g each of wheat and rye flour, 100 g milk, 40 g butter, 1 sachet baking powder, 1 tsp each of cinnamon, ginger and quatre-épices, 40 minutes at 160°C; no anise and no salt.

recipes.name: Pissaladière
recipes.flavorProfile: A thick bed of onions stewed in olive oil until soft and sweet, crossed with salty anchovies and dotted with small black olives on an olive-oil bread base.
recipes.healthBenefit: The onions bring fibre and plant compounds, the anchovies bring protein and omega-3 fats and the fat is olive oil; it is salty, so one slice beside a salad is plenty.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

ingredients.prepNote: dried, for the dough; the source gives no amount

instructions: Dough: dissolve the yeast and the teaspoon of sugar in the warm water. Mix with the flour, the 2 tsp salt, the dried thyme and 10 tbsp olive oil and knead 10 minutes until smooth. Cover and leave to rise 1 to 1.5 hours, until doubled.

Onions: meanwhile warm 5 tbsp olive oil in a wide heavy pan, add the onions, garlic, 10 g sugar and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook over low heat, stirring now and then, until the onions are very soft and pale gold; add a spoon of water if they catch. Season with pepper.
Heat the oven to 430°F (220°C). Oil a baking tray about 30 by 40 cm and press the dough out to fill it, leaving a slightly thicker rim.
Spread the onions over the dough. Lay the anchovy fillets in a lattice over the top and set an olive in each diamond.
Bake 10 minutes at 430°F (220°C), then 5 to 10 minutes at 375°F (190°C), until the base is crisp and golden underneath. Serve warm or at room temperature, cut into 8 slices.

nutritionHighlights.note: High, from the anchovies and olives.

recipes.curationNote: 750g, Pissaladière for every amount and step; one 30 by 40 cm tray: dough of 500 g flour, 20 cl water, 15 g fresh yeast, 10 tbsp olive oil, 2 tsp salt, 1 tsp sugar and dried thyme with no amount; topping of 8 large onions, 3 garlic cloves, 10 g sugar, olive oil, salt, pepper, a can of anchovies and olives; 10 minutes at 220°C then 5 to 10 at 190°C. Followed in full rather than blended with Wikipédia.

recipes.name: Pain de Mie
recipes.flavorProfile: A soft square sandwich loaf with a fine, tight, very white crumb and a thin soft crust, mild and faintly milky.
recipes.healthBenefit: Milk adds a little protein and calcium and there is only a little butter and sugar; it is a white bread, so it is best toasted with eggs or used for a sandwich with plenty of filling.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.cutPrep: melted, plus a little for the tin

instructions: Mix the yeast with the warm milk and sugar. Add the flour, salt and melted butter and knead at least 10 minutes by hand, or 6 to 8 by machine, until smooth and elastic.
Cover and rise 1 hour somewhere warm, until doubled.

Knock back, flatten into a rectangle the length of a buttered loaf tin (a lidded pain de mie tin if you have one) and roll it up tightly. Set it seam down in the tin and proof about 45 minutes, until doubled. With a lid, slide it on when the dough is 1 cm below the rim.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) and bake 25 to 30 minutes. Turn the loaf out for the last 5 minutes and put it back in the oven on the rack so the base and sides colour lightly.
Cool completely on a rack before slicing into about 16 slices.
recipes.curationNote: 750g, Pain de mie for every amount and step; 450 g flour, 230 ml water, apple juice or milk, 20 g melted margarine, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp dry yeast, 2 tsp salt; 200°C for 30 minutes. Butter is kept in place of margarine as the curation chose, at the source's amount.

recipes.name: Crème Brûlée
recipes.flavorProfile: A cold, silky vanilla custard under a thin sheet of burnt sugar that cracks under the spoon and tastes faintly bitter against the cream.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat built on cream and egg yolks, so it is heavy in saturated fat and sugar; the yolks do bring choline and vitamin A, and a small ramekin is the right amount.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.prepNote: about 1 tbsp; or the seeds of 1 vanilla pod, as the method describes

instructions: Heat the oven to 285°F (140°C). Warm the milk and cream with the split vanilla pod and its seeds until steaming, then take off the heat and leave to infuse 10 to 15 minutes.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar just until pale; do not beat in air. Pour the warm cream over them slowly, stirring, then strain out the pod.
Pour into 4 shallow ramekins and set them in a deep tray. Add hot water to come halfway up the sides.
Bake 35 to 45 minutes, until the edges are set and the centres still tremble. Cool, then chill at least 3 hours or overnight.
Just before serving, scatter the brown sugar thinly over each and caramelize with a kitchen torch, or 1 to 2 minutes under a very hot grill. Let the crust harden 1 to 2 minutes.

nutritionHighlights.note: Four yolks across four ramekins give each serving a good share of the day's choline.
Cream and yolks both carry vitamin A, which needs the fat around it to be absorbed.

recipes.curationNote: Proportions follow Géraldine (4 yolks, 50 g sugar, milk and cream, a vanilla pod, a water bath at 140°C). Wikipédia confirms the yolk, sugar, cream and vanilla custard with cassonade on top, first written down by Massialot in 1691.

recipes.name: Mousse au Chocolat
recipes.flavorProfile: Deep, slightly bitter dark chocolate made light by beaten egg whites, cool and airy on the tongue and dense at the bottom of the glass.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat; dark chocolate brings iron, magnesium and cocoa flavanols, and the eggs add protein, but the raw eggs mean very fresh eggs, and none for pregnancy or anyone immune-compromised.
instructions: Melt the chocolate gently over barely simmering water, or in short bursts in the microwave, and let it cool to just warm, about 5 minutes.
Stir the yolks and vanilla into the chocolate one yolk at a time until glossy.
Whisk the whites with the salt to soft peaks, then add the sugar and keep whisking to firm, glossy peaks.
Stir a third of the whites into the chocolate to loosen it, then fold in the rest gently in two additions until no white streaks remain.
Spoon into 4 glasses or one bowl and chill 2 to 4 hours, until set.

nutritionHighlights.note: Dark chocolate is one of the richer everyday sources of magnesium.
The chocolate carries a fair amount of non-heme iron.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine gives 4 eggs to 150 g dark chocolate with a little sugar and no cream, which is the classic French home mousse. Wikipédia describes it as chocolate lightened with beaten whites, recorded by Menon in 1755.

components.note: one round of shortcrust, rolled to fit the pan

recipes.name: Tarte Tatin
recipes.flavorProfile: Apples cooked down in dark butter caramel until soft and amber, turned out over a crisp pastry base, sweet with a burnt-sugar edge.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat with a lot of sugar and butter; the apples bring some fibre and potassium, and a thin slice is plenty.

ingredients.cutPrep: about 6 firm apples, peeled, cored and quartered

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Roll the pastry into a round a little wider than a 26 cm ovenproof skillet and chill it while you make the caramel.
Spread the sugar in the dry skillet over medium heat and leave it to melt and turn amber, 6 to 8 minutes, swirling rather than stirring. Take off the heat and stir in the butter.
Pack the apple quarters in tightly, rounded side down, in concentric circles. Return to medium heat and cook 10 to 15 minutes, until the juices bubble and darken.
Lay the pastry over the apples and tuck the edge down inside the pan. Prick it a few times.
Bake 45 to 50 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden. Rest 5 to 10 minutes, then lay a plate on top and turn the tart out in one move. Serve warm, with crème fraîche if you like.

nutritionHighlights.note: About six apples go into the tart, so each slice carries some fibre.
The cooked apples hold their potassium.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine bakes 6 apples in a dry caramel of 120 g sugar and 50 g butter in a 26 cm pan at 180°C, then turns it out. Wikipédia names the Tatin sisters at Lamotte-Beuvron and allows puff, sablée or brisée pastry; the shortcrust base is used here.

components.note: about half a batch, rolled 3 mm thin

recipes.name: Tarte Fine aux Pommes
recipes.flavorProfile: A crisp, shattering sheet of puff pastry under fanned, paper-thin apple slices with caramelized edges and a light brown sugar glaze.
recipes.healthBenefit: A treat made of butter pastry and sugar; the thin layer of apple adds a little fibre and potassium.

ingredients.cutPrep: about 3 apples, peeled, cored and sliced 2 mm thin

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Roll the puff pastry 3 mm thin, cut a 28 cm round or a long rectangle, and lay it on a lined tray. Prick it all over and chill 15 minutes.
Overlap the apple slices in tight rows or a rosette, leaving a 1 cm border.
Scatter the brown sugar over the apples.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes, until the pastry is puffed and golden and the apple edges have browned. Serve warm.

nutritionHighlights.note: The apple slices add a modest amount of fibre.

recipes.curationNote: La Cuisine de Géraldine, French apple tart for every amount and step; serves 6: puff pastry, about 400 g thinly sliced apples and 1 tbsp brown sugar over a layer of applesauce, 180°C for 35 to 40 minutes; no butter or lemon. The applesauce layer is left out, since a tarte fine is the thin version of this tart with apples only.

recipes.name: Clafoutis aux Cerises
recipes.flavorProfile: Dark sweet cherries baked into a soft, eggy, lightly sweet batter, somewhere between a flan and a pancake, with a faint almond note from the pits.
recipes.healthBenefit: Lighter than most French desserts, made with milk rather than cream; the cherries bring vitamin C and polyphenols and the eggs and milk add protein and calcium.

ingredients.cutPrep: stemmed, pits left in as in Limousin

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Butter a 23 cm baking dish and dust it with the 10 g of sugar.
Spread the cherries in the dish in one layer.
Whisk the eggs with the 75 g sugar, then whisk in the flour until smooth and add the milk a little at a time until the batter is thin.
Pour the batter over the cherries and bake 35 to 40 minutes, until puffed and golden and set in the centre.
Serve warm or at room temperature, warning everyone about the pits.

nutritionHighlights.note: Half a kilo of cherries gives each serving some vitamin C.
The milk in the batter adds calcium.
Three eggs and the milk give it more protein than a cake.

recipes.curationNote: La Cuisine de Géraldine, Cherry clafoutis for every amount and step; for 6 like ours: 500 g cherries, 3 eggs, 100 g flour, 75 g sugar, 300 ml milk, an optional 1 tsp flavoring, 1 tsp butter and 1 tbsp sugar for the dish; no salt.

recipes.name: Crêpes Suzette
recipes.flavorProfile: Thin warm crêpes folded into quarters and soaked in a glossy orange butter caramel, bright with zest and warmed by orange liqueur.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat of butter, sugar and liqueur; the orange juice brings a little vitamin C, and the alcohol mostly stays if it is not flamed for long.
instructions: Cook 8 thin crêpes from the batter, 1 to 2 minutes a side, and stack them.

In a wide frying pan melt the sugar over medium heat until it turns light amber, 3 to 5 minutes. Add the butter, then the orange juice and zest, and stir until the caramel dissolves into a smooth sauce, 2 to 3 minutes.
One at a time, lay each crêpe in the sauce for about 30 seconds, turn it, then fold it in half and in half again and push it to the side of the pan.
Pour in the liqueur and let it bubble 30 seconds to 1 minute. To flame it, tilt the pan away from you and light it with a long match, standing well back, and let the flames die out.
Serve 2 crêpes per plate with the sauce spooned over.

nutritionHighlights.note: The fresh orange juice and zest carry some vitamin C.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine makes the sauce from 50 g sugar, 60 g butter, two oranges and 3 cl Grand Marnier, soaking each crêpe about 30 seconds. Wikipédia names the beurre Suzette and Grand Marnier or curaçao, and ties the dish to Escoffier around 1890. The database holds a general liqueur, used for Grand Marnier.

recipes.name: Crêpes au Sucre
recipes.flavorProfile: Hot, thin, lacy crêpes with a smear of melting butter and a crunch of sugar, the plain street crêpe of France.
recipes.healthBenefit: A simple treat of white flour, butter and sugar with egg and milk in the batter for a little protein and calcium.

ingredients.prepNote: juice of half a lemon; optional, squeezed over

instructions: Heat a crêpe pan or 24 cm frying pan over medium high heat and wipe it with a little butter.
Pour in a small ladle of batter and tilt the pan to cover the base thinly. Cook 1 to 2 minutes, until the edge lifts and the underside is speckled gold, then flip and cook 30 seconds to 1 minute.
While the crêpe is still in the pan, rub a little butter over it and scatter about 1 tsp of sugar, with a few drops of lemon if you like.
Fold in half and then in half again and serve straight away. Repeat with the rest of the batter.

nutritionHighlights.note: The milk in the batter adds some calcium.

recipes.curationNote: Batter proportions follow Géraldine and the shared crêpe base. Wikipédia describes crêpes eaten hot with butter and sugar added once they are cooked, the everyday way and the one served at Chandeleur.

recipes.name: Profiteroles
recipes.flavorProfile: Crisp, hollow little choux puffs filled with cold vanilla ice cream and drowned in warm, glossy dark chocolate sauce.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat of butter, egg, cream and sugar; the dark chocolate adds a little iron and magnesium.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C), the base choux recipe's temperature, since the source gives none. Pipe the choux paste into puffs 4 to 5 cm across on a tray lined with baking paper.
Bake about 30 minutes, until puffed and golden, without opening the door for the first 20 minutes. Cool on a rack.
For the sauce, bring the milk to a simmer and pour it over the chopped chocolate. Cover, wait 30 seconds, then stir smooth with a spatula.
Cut the puffs in half, fill each with a scoop of vanilla ice cream, close them and serve with the hot sauce.

nutritionHighlights.note: The dark chocolate sauce adds a little iron.

recipes.name: Éclairs au Chocolat
recipes.flavorProfile: Long, crisp choux fingers split with a cool, thick chocolate pastry cream and topped with a shiny chocolate fondant glaze.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich pastry of butter, egg, milk and sugar; the dark chocolate brings a little iron and magnesium and the pastry cream some calcium.

ingredients.cutPrep: chopped, stirred into the warm pastry cream

instructions: Make the crème pâtissière and, while it is still hot, stir in the chopped chocolate until melted. Cover the surface and chill at least 2 hours.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Pipe the choux paste into 12 fingers about 12 cm long and 2.5 cm wide on a lined tray.
Bake 40 to 50 minutes, until deep golden and dry, without opening the door in the first 25 minutes. Cool on a rack.
Make 2 or 3 small holes underneath each éclair and pipe in the chocolate cream until each feels heavy.

Warm the fondant with the cocoa and a little water over low heat to about 95°F (35°C), until it flows. Dip the top of each éclair, wipe the edge, and let it set 15 to 20 minutes. Keep chilled and eat within the day.

nutritionHighlights.note: The milk in the pastry cream adds calcium.
Chocolate in both the cream and glaze adds a little iron.

recipes.name: Paris-Brest
recipes.flavorProfile: A wheel of crisp choux pastry scattered with toasted flaked almonds, split and piped full of a rich, nutty hazelnut praline butter cream.
recipes.healthBenefit: A very rich treat of butter, sugar and eggs; the almonds and hazelnuts add vitamin E and some magnesium.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: For the praline paste, toast the hazelnuts and whole almonds at 325°F (160°C) for 10 to 12 minutes. Melt the 53 g of sugar in a dry pan to an amber caramel, stir in the warm nuts, spread on a lined tray to harden, then break up and blend to a smooth paste.

For the cream, warm the milk with the vanilla. Whisk the yolks with the 27 g of sugar, then the cornflour. Pour in the hot milk gradually, return it to the pan and cook about 2 minutes. Cover the surface with film and chill at least 2 hours.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Pipe the choux through a large plain tip into two 20 cm rings side by side, then a third ring on top of the join. Scatter the flaked almonds over.
Bake 40 to 45 minutes, until deep golden and firm, without opening the door for the first 25 minutes. Cool on a rack and slice in half horizontally with a bread knife.
Whisk the very cold cream with the praline paste, then whisk in the soft butter a little at a time until smooth.
Pipe the praline cream through a fluted tip over the bottom ring, set the top on, dust with icing sugar and chill until serving.

nutritionHighlights.note: Hazelnuts and almonds are among the richest food sources of vitamin E.

recipes.name: Madeleines
recipes.flavorProfile: Small shell-shaped butter cakes with crisp golden edges, a soft, fine, honeyed crumb, a hint of lemon and the classic hump on top.
recipes.healthBenefit: A small butter and sugar treat; one madeleine is a modest portion.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

ingredients.cutPrep: melted and cooled, plus a little for the tin

instructions: Whisk the eggs, sugar and honey until pale and foamy, 3 to 5 minutes. Stir in the lemon zest.
Fold in the flour, baking powder and salt, then the cooled melted butter, until smooth.
Cover and chill the batter at least 2 hours, or overnight. The cold batter against a hot oven gives the hump.
Butter and flour a madeleine tin. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Fill each shell three quarters full.
Bake 4 minutes, then lower the oven to 350°F (180°C) and bake another 6 to 8 minutes, until golden at the edges and springy. Turn out at once and eat warm or the same day.

nutritionHighlights.note: The butter and eggs bring a little vitamin A.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine makes 15 madeleines from 2 eggs, 100 g sugar, a spoon of honey, 150 g flour, 125 g butter, baking powder and lemon zest, chilled 2 hours and started at 220°C. Wikipédia names Commercy in Lorraine and the same ingredients.

recipes.name: Financiers
recipes.flavorProfile: Small, moist almond cakes with a crisp golden crust and a chewy, nutty crumb tasting of browned butter.
recipes.healthBenefit: A butter and sugar treat; the ground almonds add vitamin E and some magnesium, and the egg whites a little protein.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

instructions: Melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat and cook 4 to 6 minutes, until it smells nutty and the solids at the bottom turn hazelnut brown. Strain and let it cool to warm.
Mix the icing sugar, ground almonds, flour and salt. Stir in the egg whites and vanilla until smooth, without beating in air.
Stir in the browned butter until glossy. Chill the batter 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Butter 8 financier or small rectangular moulds and fill them three quarters full.
Bake 15 to 18 minutes, until golden brown at the edges and springy in the centre. Cool 5 minutes, then turn out.
recipes.curationNote: Géraldine makes 8 from 100 g browned butter, 100 g icing sugar, 75 g ground almonds, 40 g flour and 3 whites, chilled 30 minutes and baked at 180°C. Wikipédia gives the same beurre noisette, almond powder, white and icing sugar cake, recorded by Lacam in 1865.

recipes.name: Île Flottante
recipes.flavorProfile: Soft clouds of poached meringue floating on cold vanilla custard, laced with threads of crisp amber caramel and toasted almonds.
recipes.healthBenefit: Lighter than it looks, since the meringue is mostly egg white, but the custard and caramel make it a sweet treat; the yolks bring choline and the milk calcium.
instructions: Chill the crème anglaise at least 2 hours.
Whisk the whites to soft peaks, then add the icing sugar and whisk to firm, glossy peaks.
Bring a wide pan of water to a bare simmer. Drop in large spoonfuls of meringue, a few at a time, and poach 2 to 3 minutes, then turn them and poach 1 minute more. Lift onto a clean cloth to drain.
Pour the custard into 6 shallow bowls and set the meringues on top. Chill until serving.

For the caramel, melt the sugar alone in a dry pan over medium heat, without stirring, until amber, 6 to 8 minutes. Off the heat, drizzle it in thin threads over the meringues with a fork and scatter the toasted almonds over.

nutritionHighlights.note: Five egg whites give the meringue protein with almost no fat.

recipes.curationNote: La Cuisine de Géraldine, Île flottante for every amount and step; for 6 like ours: 5 whites with 50 g icing sugar poached in simmering water, a 5 yolk crème anglaise, ⅓ cup sugar melted to caramel with no water, toasted sliced almonds; no salt.

recipes.name: Far Breton
recipes.flavorProfile: A dense, custardy, slightly chewy flan baked dark on top and studded with soft prunes, with a buttery edge from the salted butter in the dish.
recipes.healthBenefit: A sweet treat, though made with milk rather than cream; the prunes bring fibre, potassium and vitamin K, and the eggs and milk add protein and calcium.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C) with the fan on. Butter a 24 cm round or 20 by 30 cm baking dish with the salted butter and scatter the prunes in it.
Whisk the eggs with the sugar and salt, then whisk in the flour until smooth. Add the milk gradually to a thin batter.
Pour the batter over the prunes.
Bake 45 to 50 minutes, until golden on top and still slightly wobbly in the centre; it sinks as it cools.
Cool to room temperature before slicing, or chill it, which firms the texture.

nutritionHighlights.note: A quarter kilo of prunes gives each slice a share of fibre.
The three quarters of a litre of milk adds calcium.

recipes.name: Tarte au Citron
recipes.flavorProfile: A crisp, buttery sweet pastry shell filled with a smooth, sharp, silky lemon curd, tart first and then sweet.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat of butter, sugar and eggs; the fresh lemon brings vitamin C and the eggs protein and choline.
instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Line a 23 cm tart tin with the pastry, prick it, line with paper and baking beans, and blind bake 15 minutes. Remove the beans and bake 5 to 10 minutes more, until golden. Cool.
Whisk the sugar, eggs and cornstarch in a saucepan, then whisk in the lemon juice and zest.
Cook over medium low heat, whisking all the time, until it thickens and the first bubbles break the surface, 5 to 8 minutes. Take off the heat.
Whisk in the butter a few cubes at a time until smooth and glossy. Strain if you want it very fine.
Pour into the cooled shell, smooth the top, and chill at least 4 hours before slicing.

nutritionHighlights.note: The juice of five lemons gives each slice some vitamin C.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine blind bakes a sweet pastry at 180°C and fills it with a curd of 150 g sugar, 4 eggs, 20 g cornstarch, 175 ml lemon juice with zest and 100 g butter, chilled at least 4 hours. Wikipédia describes the same pastry and lemon cream tart and its ties to Menton. Her pastry adds ground almonds; the shared pâte sucrée is used here.

recipes.name: Macarons
recipes.flavorProfile: Two smooth, crisp almond meringue shells with ruffled feet and a chewy centre, sandwiched with a white chocolate and honey ganache.
recipes.healthBenefit: A small sugary treat; the almonds add a little vitamin E, and one macaron is a light portion.
instructions: Sift the ground almonds and icing sugar together, discarding any coarse bits.
Whisk the whites to soft peaks, then add the caster sugar a little at a time and whisk to stiff, glossy peaks.
Fold the almond mixture into the meringue, then keep folding and pressing the batter against the bowl until it falls from the spatula in a thick ribbon.
Pipe 3 cm rounds on lined trays, rap the trays on the counter to release air, and leave them 20 to 40 minutes until a skin forms and they no longer stick to a finger.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C), fan, and bake 12 to 14 minutes. Cool fully.
For the ganache, heat the cream with the honey, pour it over the chopped white chocolate, stir smooth and stir in the butter. Leave 2 to 3 hours at room temperature until firm enough to pipe.
Sandwich the shells in pairs with the ganache and chill them 24 hours before eating.

nutritionHighlights.note: The ground almonds bring a little vitamin E.

citations.source: Gâteau et cuisine Rachida, Macarons à la meringue française

recipes.name: Crème Caramel
recipes.flavorProfile: A cool, wobbling vanilla custard turned out under a pool of thin, bittersweet amber caramel.
recipes.healthBenefit: A lighter custard than crème brûlée, made with milk rather than cream; the eggs bring protein and choline and the milk calcium, though the caramel adds sugar.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.prepNote: about 1 tbsp; or the seeds of 1 vanilla pod, as the method describes

instructions: Melt the 150 g caramel sugar alone in a dry pan over medium heat, without water and without stirring, swirling the pan until it is a deep amber caramel. Pour it at once into a 1.5 litre mould and tilt to coat the base.
Heat the oven to 250°F (120°C). Warm the milk with the split vanilla pod and its scraped seeds until steaming, then take off the heat.
Whisk the eggs, yolks and 100 g sugar together without making foam, pour in the warm milk while whisking, and strain out the pod.
Pour the custard over the caramel and bake for about 70 minutes, until set with a slight wobble in the middle.
Cool, then chill at least 4 hours. Run a knife around the edge and turn out onto a deep plate so the caramel runs down.

nutritionHighlights.note: A full litre of milk adds calcium.
Eggs and milk give each serving some protein.

recipes.name: Mille-Feuille
recipes.flavorProfile: Three sheets of crisp, caramelized puff pastry layered with thick vanilla pastry cream, topped with white fondant feathered with chocolate.
recipes.healthBenefit: A very rich pastry of butter, flour, milk, eggs and sugar; the pastry cream adds some calcium.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: For the cream, heat the milk with the vanilla and half the sugar. Whisk the yolks with the rest of the sugar, then whisk in the cornflour and a little of the hot milk.
Pour it all back into the pan and cook over low heat for 4 minutes, whisking. Cover the surface with film and chill it quickly, about 20 minutes in the freezer.
Beat the butter until soft, then beat it gradually into the smoothed cold cream. Spoon it into a piping bag with a plain 1 cm tip and keep it cold.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Roll the puff pastry 2 mm thick into a rectangle about 70 by 25 cm, prick it, cover with baking paper and set a rack on top.
Bake 30 minutes. Take off the top paper, dust with the icing sugar and bake 10 minutes more, until caramelised. Cut into 3 strips and cool on a rack.
Pipe cream over the first strip, cover with the second, pipe more cream and finish with the third strip.
Melt the fondant and the chocolate separately. Spread the fondant over the top, pipe lines of chocolate across it and drag a skewer or knife through them to feather.
Chill to set, then cut into 8 with a serrated knife.

nutritionHighlights.note: The milk in the pastry cream adds calcium.

recipes.name: Tarte aux Fraises
recipes.flavorProfile: A crisp sweet pastry shell spread with cool vanilla pastry cream and crowded with fresh, juicy strawberries.
recipes.healthBenefit: A treat of pastry, cream and sugar, lighter than many because of the fresh fruit; the strawberries bring plenty of vitamin C and folate.
instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Line a 23 cm tart tin with the pastry, prick it, line with paper and baking beans, and bake about 20 minutes in all, taking the beans out for the last few minutes, until golden. Cool completely.
Beat the cold crème pâtissière until smooth and spread it evenly in the shell.
Arrange the strawberries close together over the cream, points up.
Chill up to 2 hours before serving. It is best eaten the day it is made.

nutritionHighlights.note: The fresh strawberries give each slice a good share of vitamin C.

recipes.name: Canelés

recipes.healthBenefit: A small sugary treat; the milk and eggs add a little protein and calcium.

ingredients.prepNote: about 1 tbsp; or the seeds of 1 vanilla pod, as the method describes

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

instructions: Bring the milk to a boil with the vanilla pod and seeds and the 50 g butter, then take off the heat.
Mix the sugar and flour, then stir in the egg and yolks. Pour in the hot milk gradually, stirring without beating, until smooth. Cool, add the rum, and remove the pod.
Cover and chill the batter 24 to 48 hours.
Heat the oven to 465°F (240°C). Brush copper or silicone canelé moulds with the melted butter. Stir the batter gently and fill the moulds to 1 cm from the top.
Bake 10 minutes, then lower to 350°F (180°C) and bake 45 to 55 minutes, until the crusts are a deep mahogany. Turn out at once and cool on a rack; they are crispest within a few hours.

recipes.flavorProfile: Pear halves poached soft in a light sugar syrup, served cold with vanilla ice cream and warm, glossy dark chocolate sauce poured over at the table.

Put a layer of vanilla ice cream in each bowl, set 2 pear halves on top and coat with the warm chocolate sauce. Scatter with flaked almonds if you like.

The dark chocolate adds some magnesium.

recipes.name: Gâteau Basque
recipes.flavorProfile: A crumbly, buttery almond shortbread crust baked golden around a thick layer of rum and vanilla pastry cream.

ingredients.cutPrep: 100 g for the dough, 40 g for the cream

ingredients.prepNote: 3 g for the dough, a pinch for the glaze

ingredients.cutPrep: one for the dough, one beaten to glaze

ingredients.prepNote: zest of a quarter of a lemon

Bake 40 to 50 minutes, turning the cake halfway, until deep golden. Cool fully in the tin before slicing.

instructions: Dissolve the yeast in the water and mix with the flour and salt. Knead 5 to 8 minutes to a smooth dough. Cover and rise 1 hour, until doubled.
Beat the cold salted butter flat between sheets of paper into a 15 cm square. Roll the dough into a 30 cm square, set the butter in the middle and fold the corners over it to enclose it.

Roll into a long rectangle and fold in three. Chill 20 to 30 minutes. Roll and fold again, scattering a third of the sugar over before folding. Repeat twice more, until all the sugar is in, chilling between turns if the butter softens.

Bake about 35 minutes, until deep amber and caramelized. Turn out onto a rack after 5 minutes, before the caramel sets in the tin. Eat warm or the same day.
